text: Nine lessons ago, Priya asked a vague question: what happens if this database disappears? Let's recap the specific, real thing you built in answer.

You turned a vague fear into one testable requirement, planned a real backup strategy, and deployed the actual Azure SQL Database it protects. Then you confirmed the full, differential, and log backup chains Azure runs automatically on this platform — not guessed at them, confirmed them. And then came the real work: you actually restored the database to a point in time, wrote a two-part health check, and documented all of it as a runbook a teammate could follow.

Here's what made this project real instead of theoretical. Overlook's old maintenance plan showed success for two years and had never once been restored. This project's Lesson 7 was different — an actual restore, actually verified. That's the one non-negotiable step a beginner capstone could have skipped by just describing the concept. This one didn't.

It's worth being honest about what's still missing. There's no high-availability or geo-replication — Overlook's database still has a single point of failure at the region level. There's no automated alerting — the health check is something a human runs. And it's one database only; other Overlook systems deserve this same treatment eventually. None of that is a failure of this project — it's the honest edge of a beginner-scoped one.

The Intermediate-tier capstone picks up right where this one leaves off. Overlook now has two departments and a growing performance problem, not just a recoverability one. The backup discipline you built here doesn't go away — it's the foundation the next project stands on.
